### Problem: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array {#sec-lts-p2-a}

::: {.p-statement}

Given `nums` of length $n$ where each $\mathit{nums}[i] \in [1, n]$ ($1 \le n \le 10^5$), return every integer in $[1, n]$ that does **not** appear. Follow-up (the real point): do it in $O(n)$ time and *without extra space* — the returned list doesn't count.

Source: [LC 448 · Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}

Example — `nums = [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1]`. Output `[5, 6]`.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A hash set of $1..n$ minus the values works, but the follow-up forbids it. The promise $\mathit{nums}[i] \in [1, n]$ is the giveaway: the array has exactly one slot per possible value, so it *can be its own set*. Walk each value, and use it (via $x-1$) as an index to "flag" that value as seen — flip the sign of the cell it points at. The un-flagged cells are the missing numbers.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Set difference.** Build `set(nums)`; report the $v \in [1, n]$ not in it. $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space — correct but uses the space the follow-up bans.
2. **Sign marking.** For each $x$, go to slot $|x|-1$ and make it negative if not already. Afterwards, slot $i$ still positive means value $i+1$ was never pointed at — collect it. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space.

**Invariant.** After the marking pass, `nums[i] < 0` if and only if some element equalled $i+1$; signs are idempotent, so duplicates just re-mark the same slot and never corrupt it.
:::

The buttons are in order: reach for a hash set, then realise the array can store its own set.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Set difference

::: {.form-next}
Collect the values into a set, then list the numbers in $[1, n]$ the set lacks. $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space — the oracle and the very space budget the follow-up removes.

**Worked example.** $\{1,2,3,4,7,8\}$ present; of $1..8$ the absent ones are $5, 6$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("disapp", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "[5, 6]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def fad448_set(nums):
    have = set(nums)
    return [v for v in range(1, len(nums) + 1) if v not in have]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// set of 1..n minus the values present, O(n) time O(n) space
vector<int> fad448Set(vector<int> nums) {
    unordered_set<int> have(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    vector<int> ans;
    for (int v = 1; v <= (int)nums.size(); ++v)
        if (!have.count(v)) ans.push_back(v);
    return ans;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** Hashing values into a set is the general "which of these did I see" tool (@sec-hash), costing $O(n)$ memory. Here the values are already *known* to be indices $1..n$, so a boolean-per-slot would do the same job for $O(n)$ space with no hashing — and the sign-marking form shrinks even that to $O(1)$ by borrowing the array's own sign bit as the flag.

#### Sign marking (O(1) extra space)

::: {.form-next}
For every element $x$, jump to slot $|x|-1$ and negate it (skip if already negative). Then every index $i$ whose cell is still positive marks a value $i+1$ nobody pointed at. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space.

**Worked example.** Marking $[4,3,2,7,8,2,3,1]$ leaves slots 4 and 5 positive → missing $[5, 6]$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("disapp", "sign")
    assert str(final) == "[5, 6]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-448-sign
def fad448_sign(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    a = list(nums)
    for x in nums:
        idx = abs(x) - 1
        if a[idx] > 0:
            a[idx] = -a[idx]
    return [i + 1 for i in range(n) if a[i] > 0]

for _ in range(400):
    n = random.randint(1, 30)
    x = [random.randint(1, n) for _ in range(n)]
    assert fad448_sign(x) == fad448_set(x)
assert fad448_sign([4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1]) == [5, 6]
assert fad448_sign([1, 1]) == [2]
print("fad448_sign OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// mark "seen" by negating the pointed-at cell; O(1) extra space
vector<int> fad448Sign(vector<int> nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    for (int x : nums) {
        int idx = abs(x) - 1;
        if (nums[idx] > 0) nums[idx] = -nums[idx];
    }
    vector<int> ans;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        if (nums[i] > 0) ans.push_back(i + 1);
    return ans;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `abs(x)` is essential in the second pass because cells have already been flipped negative — we read the *original* value by magnitude. The Python version copies into `a` to keep the stress test's input reusable; the C++ version mutates its by-value parameter. Notice the array became a histogram of presence ($0$ or $\ge 1$ per bucket), stored entirely in its own sign bits — the purest example of "the value is the address."

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Set difference** is $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space. **Sign marking** is $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space (the answer list excluded). Both are linear; the second spends no memory because the value range $[1, n]$ lets the array index itself.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- All equal `[1,1,...,1]`: slot 0 marked, every other slot stays positive → the whole tail $[2..n]$ is missing.
- Full permutation (each once): nothing missing → `[]`.
- `n = 1`: the single value is `1`, so `[]`; a value outside `[1, n]` cannot occur by the constraint.
:::

- [LC 268 · Missing Number](https://leetcode.com/problems/missing-number/){difficulty="Easy"} — values $0..n$ with one gap: sign marking, cyclic placement, or a sum.
:::
